[tryit] Show a grown-up how you wash your hands.

b2-comp-1: Writes an algorithm (step-by-step instructions) for an everyday task
b2-comp-3: Finds and fixes a bug in a short set of instructions (debugging)
column9:
[text] An ALGORITHM is a list of steps to do a job, like a recipe.

[text] Computers follow algorithms exactly. They can't guess what we mean!

[text] A mistake in the steps is called a BUG. 🐞 Finding and fixing it is called DEBUGGING.

[text] Example: 'Brush teeth: 1. Rinse. 2. Brush. 3. Put toothpaste on brush.' The bug: step 3 should come before step 2!

[tryit] Write an algorithm for making a glass of water. Ask someone to follow it exactly. Any bugs?

[parent] Following instructions literally ('you said pick up the cup, not fill it!') makes this lesson memorable and funny.

[text] The number 23 has 2 tens and 3 ones.

[text] To add 23 + 15, add the tens first. 2 tens + 1 ten = 3 tens. That is 30.

[text] Then add the ones. 3 + 5 = 8. So 30 + 8 = 38!

b2-money-2: Understands needs vs wants

[text] A WANT is something nice to have, but we can live without it: toys, sweets, games.

column5: b2-sci-3: Knows the states of matter: solid, liquid, gas
column9:
[text] Everything around us is made of matter. Matter can be a solid, a liquid or a gas.

[text] A SOLID keeps its shape. A rock, a spoon and ice are solids. 🧊

[text] A LIQUID flows and takes the shape of its cup. Water and juice are liquids. 💧

[text] A GAS spreads out to fill any space. The air we breathe is a gas. 🎈

[fact] Water can be all three! Ice (solid), water (liquid) and steam (gas).

[tryit] With a grown-up: put an ice cube on a plate. Check it every 10 minutes. What happens?

[parent] Supervise any activity with hot water or steam. Ask 'does it keep its shape?' to help your child sort things.

[text] Opinions are fine to have. But it's good to know when something is an opinion.

[fact] Some countries teach six continents, joining North and South America, or Europe and Asia. Both ways are OK!

[text] The five oceans are: Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic. The Pacific is the biggest.

b3-dig-2: Recognises scams, fake prizes and suspicious links
b3-dig-1: Creates strong passwords and never shares them
column9:
[text] A scam is a trick to get your money, your passwords or your personal information.

[text] Warning signs: 'You WON a prize!', 'Hurry, only 5 minutes left!', 'Click this link to claim', or messages asking for passwords or codes.

[text] Scammers use excitement or fear to make you act fast without thinking.

[text] The rule: STOP, don't click, and show a trusted adult.

[fact] Real companies will never ask for your password in a message.

b3-health-4: Understands stress and healthy ways to cope
b3-health-3: Friendship skills, dealing with bullying, asking for help
column9:
[text] Everyone feels stressed, worried or angry sometimes. Feelings aren't bad. They're signals from your body and brain.

[text] Stress can show up in your body: a fast heartbeat, a tummy ache, tight shoulders or trouble sleeping.

[text] Calm-down tools: slow breathing (in for 4, out for 6), moving your body, drawing or writing, going somewhere quiet, or a hug.

[text] Talking helps! Tell a parent, teacher or friend what's on your mind. Big problems feel smaller when you share them.

[fact] Breathing out slowly helps your body calm down.

[text] If worries don't go away, or you ever feel unsafe, tell a trusted adult. Getting help is brave, not weak.

[tryit] Try 'box breathing': breathe in for 4, hold for 4, out for 4, hold for 4. Do it 4 times. How do you feel?

column5:
b3-lang-1: Reads texts of a few paragraphs independently and finds the main idea and supporting details (GPF G4–6)
b3-lang-2: Makes inferences: works out what is not said directly
column9:
[text] The MAIN IDEA is what a paragraph is mostly about. The other sentences are DETAILS that support it.

[text] The main idea is often in the first sentence (the topic sentence), but not always. Sometimes it's at the end, or not written at all.

[text] Test: ask 'What is this mostly about?' Then check: do most sentences support your answer?

[fact] Example: 'Octopuses are amazing escape artists. They can squeeze through tiny gaps. They change colour to hide. Some even squirt ink.' Main idea: octopuses are good at escaping. Everything else is a detail.

[text] An INFERENCE is working out something the writer doesn't say directly, using clues in the text.

[tryit] Pick a paragraph from any book. Write its main idea in 10 words or fewer.

column5: b3-math-2: Understands, compares and adds fractions; links fractions, decimals and percentages
column9:
[text] A fraction like 3/4 means 3 parts out of 4 equal parts. The bottom number (denominator) says how many parts the whole is cut into.

[text] Same denominator? Just compare the tops. 5/8 is bigger than 3/8 because 5 pieces is more than 3 pieces of the same size.

[text] Same numerator? The SMALLER denominator wins! 1/3 is bigger than 1/5, because a pizza cut into 3 has bigger slices than one cut into 5.

[text] Different tops and bottoms? Make the denominators the same. For 2/3 and 3/4, use twelfths: 2/3 = 8/12 and 3/4 = 9/12. So 3/4 is bigger.

[tryit] Fold two paper strips the same length. Fold one into 3 parts and one into 4. Shade 2/3 and 3/4 and compare.

b3-money-1: Makes a simple budget for pocket money

column9:
[text] A BUDGET is a plan for your money. It shows money coming in (income) and money going out (spending).

[text] A simple plan: split money into Save, Spend and Share (giving to others or charity).

[text] Example: you get 50 coins. Save 20, spend 25, share 5. Total = 50. A budget must add up!

[text] Comparing prices helps your money go further. Bigger isn't always cheaper. Work out the cost of each item.

[fact] Many adults use the same idea, with more categories like rent, food and travel.

column5: b3-sci-4: Knows the water cycle and the solar system
column9:
[text] The water you drink today may once have been in an ocean, a cloud or a glacier. Earth keeps reusing its water in a loop called the water cycle.

[text] 1. Evaporation: the Sun heats water in oceans, lakes and rivers. It turns into water vapour, a gas, and rises.

[text] 2. Condensation: high up, the air is cooler. The vapour cools into tiny droplets that form clouds.

[text] 3. Precipitation: droplets join and get heavy. They fall as rain, snow, sleet or hail.

[text] 4. Collection: water gathers in oceans, rivers, lakes and underground. Then the cycle starts again.

[tryit] Breathe on a cold mirror or window. The foggy patch is condensation: water vapour from your breath turning into droplets.

column2: Break a Big Problem into Small Steps
column5: b3-think-1: Breaks a big problem into smaller steps
column9:
[text] Big problems can feel scary. A powerful trick is to break them into small steps. Programmers call this DECOMPOSITION.

[text] Example: 'Plan a class party' becomes: pick a date, make a guest list, choose food, plan games, clean up.

[text] Each small step is easier to solve. Then you put the pieces together.

[text] In math word problems: 1) What do I know? 2) What am I asked? 3) What steps get me there? 4) Does my answer make sense?

[tryit] Pick a goal (like tidying your room or building a model). Break it into at least 5 small steps.

column2: Festivals of Light Around the World
column5: b3-world-5: Beliefs and practices of world religions and non-religious worldviews, compared respectfully
column9:
[text] Many religions and cultures have festivals that use light. Here are three. People of each faith celebrate in their own ways, and not everyone celebrates.

[text] Diwali is celebrated by many Hindus, Sikhs and Jains, mostly in October or November. People light small oil lamps called diyas, and many see it as celebrating light over darkness and good over evil.

[text] Hanukkah is a Jewish festival lasting eight nights. Families light candles on a special candle holder, adding one more each night. It remembers the rededication of the Temple in Jerusalem long ago.

[text] Christmas is when Christians celebrate the birth of Jesus. Many people decorate with lights and candles. Some people celebrate Christmas as a cultural holiday too.

[tryit] Ask your family: do you have a festival you celebrate? What do you do on that day?

column5: b4-arts-2: Music: scales, chords, melody and harmony basics
column9:
[text] A SCALE is a set of notes in order, going up or down. The C major scale uses only the white keys on a piano: C D E F G A B C.

[text] MELODY is a sequence of single notes, the part you can hum. HARMONY is notes played at the same time to support the melody.

[text] A CHORD is three or more notes played together. The most common is a triad: the 1st, 3rd and 5th notes of a scale.

[text] C major chord = C, E and G (notes 1, 3 and 5 of the C major scale). Major chords often sound bright; minor chords often sound sadder.

[fact] Many popular songs use just four chords, repeated in different patterns.

column5: b4-comp-3: Binary numbers and how computers store data
column9:
[text] Computers store everything (numbers, text, photos, music) using just two digits: 0 and 1. This is BINARY.

[text] Each 0 or 1 is a BIT. 8 bits make a BYTE.

[text] In our normal (decimal) system, columns are worth 1, 10, 100… In binary, columns are worth 1, 2, 4, 8, 16… (each double the last).

[text] Binary 1011 = 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11. Add up the column values where there's a 1.

[fact] With 8 bits you can make 256 different patterns (0 to 255). That's why many old games had limits of 255!

[text] Building an app costs money: developers, servers, designers. So when an app is free, it makes money some other way.

[text] Ads: the app shows you adverts. Advertisers pay more when they can target people precisely, so many apps collect data about what you like, where you are and who you talk to.

[text] In-app purchases: the app is free to start, but extra lives, skins or features cost money (often called 'freemium').

[text] Your attention: the longer you stay, the more ads you see. That's why some apps use endless scrolling, autoplay and streaks. These designs are built to keep you hooked.

column5: b4-health-2: Nutrition, exercise and sleep for teenagers
column9:
[text] While you sleep, your brain stores what you learned that day, your body repairs itself, and you grow.

[text] Sleep experts recommend 9–12 hours a night for ages 6–12, and 8–10 hours for teenagers. Many teens get much less.

[text] Too little sleep can make it harder to focus, remember things and control your mood. It can also affect your health.

[text] Teen body clocks naturally shift later, so feeling awake at night is normal. Good habits help: a regular bedtime, a dark, cool room, and no screens for 30–60 minutes before bed.

[fact] Bright screens late at night can make it harder to fall asleep. Notifications keep your brain alert too.

column5: b4-lang-3: Understands figurative language: metaphor, simile, irony
column9:
[text] Figurative language means words that go beyond their literal meaning to create images or feelings.

[text] A SIMILE compares two things using 'like' or 'as': 'Her voice was as smooth as honey.'

[text] A METAPHOR says one thing IS another: 'Time is a thief.' (Time doesn't steal, but it takes moments from us.)

[text] IRONY is when the opposite of what's expected happens or is meant. A fire station burning down is situational irony. Saying 'Great weather!' in a storm is verbal irony.

[text] Personification gives human qualities to non-human things: 'The wind whispered through the trees.'

column5: b4-math-2: Writes and solves linear equations; understands variables
column9:
[text] An equation is a balance: both sides are equal. To find the unknown (x), do the same thing to both sides until x is alone.

[text] Undo operations in reverse order. In 3x + 4 = 19, x was multiplied by 3 and then 4 was added. So first subtract 4, then divide by 3.

[text] 3x + 4 = 19 → 3x = 15 → x = 5. Check: 3 × 5 + 4 = 19 ✓

[fact] Always check your answer by putting it back into the original equation.

column5:
b4-money-1: Budgeting, saving and simple vs compound interest
b4-money-2: Debt, loans and why 'buy now, pay later' can be risky
column9:
[text] INTEREST is money paid for using money. Banks may pay you interest on savings, and you pay interest when you borrow.

[text] SIMPLE interest is paid only on the original amount. 1,000 at 10% simple interest earns 100 every year.

[text] COMPOUND interest is paid on the original amount AND on interest already earned. 1,000 at 10%: year 1 → 1,100; year 2 → 1,210; year 3 → 1,331.

[text] Compounding helps savers grow money over time. But it also makes debts grow fast if you don't pay them off!

[fact] Rule of 72: divide 72 by the interest rate to estimate how many years it takes money to double. At 6%, about 12 years.

[tryit] Use a calculator: what does 500 become after 5 years at 8% compound interest? Multiply by 1.08 five times.

column5: b4-sci-2: Atoms, elements, compounds, the periodic table; chemical vs physical change
column9:
[text] Everything is made of tiny particles called ATOMS. An atom has a nucleus (protons and neutrons) with electrons around it.

[text] An ELEMENT is a substance made of only one kind of atom, like oxygen (O), gold (Au) or carbon (C). The periodic table lists all 118 known elements.

[text] A COMPOUND forms when atoms of two or more DIFFERENT elements are chemically bonded together. Water (H₂O) is 2 hydrogen atoms bonded to 1 oxygen atom.

[text] A compound can be very different from its elements. Sodium is a reactive metal and chlorine is a poisonous gas, but together they make table salt (NaCl).

[text] A MIXTURE is different: substances are mixed but not chemically bonded, like sand and water. You can often separate them by filtering.

[fact] Hydrogen is the most common element in the universe.

b4-think-1: Identifies common logical fallacies (straw man, false choice, bandwagon)
b4-think-2: Builds an argument: claim, evidence, reasoning
column9:
[text] A fallacy is a mistake in reasoning. It can make an argument sound convincing when it isn't. Spotting them protects you from being manipulated by ads, social media and even friends.

[text] Bandwagon: 'Everyone's doing it, so it must be right.' Popularity doesn't prove something is true or good.

[text] Straw man: twisting someone's argument into a weaker version, then attacking that. 'You want less homework? So you think school is pointless?'

[text] False choice: pretending there are only two options when there are more. 'Either you're with us or against us.'

[text] Attacking the person: criticising the speaker instead of their argument. 'Why listen to her about climate? She's only 14.'

column5: b4-world-2: Population, migration, cities, resources and trade
column9:
[text] Migration means people moving from one place to live in another, within a country or to another country. Humans have migrated throughout history.

[text] PUSH factors make people want to leave a place: few jobs, conflict, natural disasters, or lack of schools or healthcare.

[text] PULL factors attract people to a new place: jobs, safety, family already there, education or a better climate.

[text] URBANISATION is people moving from the countryside to cities. Today more than half of the world's people live in cities.

[text] Migration affects both places: new skills, cultures and foods arrive, and communities also have to adapt. People have different views about migration policy, and it's worth understanding the evidence behind each view.

column5: b5-arts-3: Copyright, Creative Commons and fair use for creators
column9:
[text] COPYRIGHT automatically protects original creative work (writing, music, art, photos, code) the moment it's made. Only the owner can copy, share or adapt it, unless they give permission.

[text] PUBLIC DOMAIN works have no copyright, usually because it expired (often decades after the creator's death, depending on the country). Anyone can use them freely.

[text] CREATIVE COMMONS (CC) licences let creators give permission in advance. BY = credit the creator. SA = share your adaptation under the same licence. NC = non-commercial use only. ND = no changes allowed.

[text] Many countries allow limited use without permission for things like criticism, teaching or parody ('fair use' in the US, 'fair dealing' in the UK, India and others). The rules differ and are narrower than many people think.

[text] Re-reading notes and highlighting feel productive but are among the least effective ways to study.

[text] Active recall (the testing effect): close the book and pull information out of memory with flashcards, practice questions, or explaining it aloud. Retrieval strengthens memory more than re-reading does.

[text] Spaced repetition (the spacing effect): review material over increasing gaps (1 day, 3 days, a week) instead of cramming it all at once.

[text] Interleaving: mix different types of problems in one session, so you learn to choose the right method, not just repeat one.

column5: b5-comp-1: Programming with data structures, algorithms and problem solving
column9:
[text] LINEAR SEARCH checks items one by one. For a list of n items it may take up to n checks. Fine for small lists, slow for huge ones.

[text] BINARY SEARCH works on a SORTED list. Check the middle item. If the target is smaller, discard the right half. If bigger, discard the left half. Repeat.

[text] Each step halves the list, so 1,000,000 sorted items need at most about 20 checks (2²⁰ ≈ 1,000,000). Linear search could need a million.

[text] Computer scientists describe this with Big-O notation: linear search is O(n); binary search is O(log n).

[fact] You use binary search when you guess a number between 1 and 100 by always guessing the middle: at most 7 guesses.

column5: b5-dig-1: Cybersecurity: two-factor authentication, phishing, account recovery
column9:
[text] Most account hacks don't need genius hackers. They use reused passwords, phishing and missing two-factor authentication.

[text] Use a different strong password for every important account. A password manager can create and remember them. A long passphrase (4+ random words) is strong and memorable.

[text] TWO-FACTOR AUTHENTICATION (2FA) adds a second step: something you have (an app code or security key) on top of something you know (your password). Even if your password leaks, the attacker usually can't log in.

[text] PHISHING: fake messages that trick you into giving passwords or codes. Red flags: urgency, odd sender addresses, links to look-alike sites, requests for codes.

[text] NEVER share a 2FA code. No real company will ask you for one. Set up recovery options (backup codes, a recovery email) before you need them.

column5: b5-health-3: First aid and CPR basics
column9:
[text] This lesson is an introduction, not a certificate. Take a hands-on first-aid course (often free or cheap from Red Cross/Red Crescent and other groups). Practice is what makes you able to help.

[text] 1. DANGER: check the area is safe for you first. 2. RESPONSE: tap the shoulders and shout 'Are you OK?'. 3. Call your local EMERGENCY NUMBER (or get someone to) and put the phone on speaker.

[text] If the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally, start CPR. Push hard and fast in the centre of the chest (about 5–6 cm deep for an adult), 100–120 times a minute, letting the chest come back up between pushes.

[text] Hands-only CPR (compressions without rescue breaths) is recommended for untrained bystanders helping an adult who collapsed. Keep going until help or an AED (defibrillator) arrives.

[text] An AED gives spoken instructions. Turn it on and follow them. It only shocks if it detects a rhythm that needs it.

[text] If someone is unresponsive but breathing normally, put them in the recovery position (on their side) and keep checking their breathing until help arrives.

column5: b5-lang-2: Writes research essays with citations and avoids plagiarism
column9:
[text] PLAGIARISM is presenting someone else's words or ideas as your own. In school and work it's taken seriously: failing an assignment, losing a job, or worse.

[text] Changing a few words (patchwriting) is still plagiarism if the ideas and structure are someone else's and you don't credit them.

[text] Avoid it by: putting exact words in quotation marks with a citation; paraphrasing in your own words AND citing the source; keeping a list of sources while you research.

[text] A citation tells readers where an idea came from (author, title, date, publisher or URL) so they can check it. Common styles are APA, MLA and Chicago.

[text] Using AI: if you use an AI tool to help, follow your school's rules and say how you used it. AI can also invent fake sources, so always check that a source really exists.

[fact] Common knowledge (e.g. 'Paris is the capital of France') usually doesn't need a citation. Statistics and specific claims do.

column5: b5-math-3: Statistics: distributions, sampling, correlation vs causation
column9:
[text] Two things are correlated when they tend to change together. That doesn't mean one causes the other.

[text] Confounding variable: a third factor causing both. Ice-cream sales and drownings both rise in summer. Ice cream doesn't cause drowning. Hot weather increases both swimming and ice-cream buying.

[text] Reverse causation: maybe B causes A, not A causes B. People who exercise more may sleep better, or people who sleep better may have more energy to exercise.

[text] Coincidence: with enough data, some unrelated things will line up by chance.

[text] How scientists test causation: randomised controlled trials. People are randomly assigned to groups so the only systematic difference is the thing being tested.

column5: b5-money-4: Investing basics: risk, diversification, avoiding scams
column9:
[text] Every real investment has risk. In general, higher possible returns come with higher risk of losing money. Anyone promising high returns with 'no risk' is a red flag.

[text] Ponzi scheme: early investors are paid with money from new investors, not real profits. It collapses when new money stops coming in.

[text] Pump-and-dump: promoters hype a cheap stock or coin on social media, the price jumps, they sell, and everyone else is left with losses.

[text] Other red flags: pressure to act now, 'secret' strategies, payments only in crypto or gift cards, and unregistered sellers.

[fact] Many countries have an official register of licensed investment firms. Check it before investing.

column5: b5-sci-3: Physics: motion, Newton's laws, waves, electricity, energy
column9:
[text] FIRST LAW (inertia): an object stays at rest, or keeps moving at a constant velocity, unless a net (unbalanced) force acts on it. That's why you lurch forward when a bus brakes suddenly.

[text] SECOND LAW: net force = mass × acceleration (F = ma). The same push accelerates a light object more than a heavy one. Force is measured in newtons (N).

[text] THIRD LAW: for every action force there is an equal and opposite reaction force. When you push on a wall, the wall pushes back on you with the same force. Rockets push gas down, and the gas pushes the rocket up.

[text] The two forces in the third law act on DIFFERENT objects, which is why they don't cancel out.

[fact] Seatbelts work against the first law: they apply the force that stops your body when the car stops suddenly.

column5:
b5-think-3: Understands cognitive biases (confirmation bias, anchoring)
b5-think-1: Evaluates arguments and evidence in news and research
column9:
[text] Cognitive biases are predictable shortcuts in thinking. They're usually helpful, but they can lead us to wrong conclusions. Everyone has them, including experts.

[text] CONFIRMATION BIAS: noticing and believing information that supports what we already think, and ignoring what doesn't.

[text] ANCHORING: relying too much on the first number we see. A 'was 200, now 99' price tag makes 99 feel cheap even if the item is worth 50.

[text] AVAILABILITY HEURISTIC: judging how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind. Plane crashes get huge news coverage, so flying feels riskier than driving, but per kilometre it's much safer.

[text] Defences: look for evidence AGAINST your view, ask 'what would change my mind?', check base rates and real data, and slow down on important decisions.

column5: b5-world-2: Economics basics: supply and demand, inflation, trade
column9:
[text] DEMAND is how much of something people want to buy at different prices. Usually, when the price goes up, people buy less.

[text] SUPPLY is how much sellers want to sell at different prices. Usually, when the price goes up, sellers want to sell more.

[text] The market price tends to settle where the amount people want to buy matches the amount offered: the EQUILIBRIUM.

[text] If demand rises (a product goes viral) and supply stays the same, prices tend to rise. If supply rises (a huge harvest), prices tend to fall.

[text] Real markets are messier: governments set rules and taxes, some sellers have lots of power, and people don't always act 'rationally'. Economists debate how much these matter.
